title: First commercial warehouse loan structure
body:
O.P.
Hi all, I'm looking at purchasing my first commercial warehouse as a long-term investment and would appreciate some advice on the best loan structure.
The property is: Purchase price: $650,000 Sold as a GST-free going concern Leased to September 2027 with 3-year and 5-year options. Net rent: $35,000 + GST + outgoings (tenant pays 100% of outgoings).
Our current financial position: PPOR worth approximately $1.5 million Existing home loan: $244,000, currently 100% offset with cash in the offset.
Separate $180,000 HISA (I'd prefer to keep this liquid, with the intention of investing around 50% into DHHF in my wife's name over time).
No other investment debt.
Rather than using the cash in the HISA as the deposit, I'm considering: Paying down the PPOR loan using the offset funds. Redrawing those funds into a separate investment loan split to partially fund the commercial purchase. Taking out a separate commercial investment loan (likely through ANZ Business Banking) for the balance. The commercial property would be purchased in my personal name.
My understanding is that, provided the redraw is structured correctly and used solely for the investment purchase, the interest on both the redrawn home loan split and the commercial loan should be tax deductible. This would also allow any rental losses to be negatively geared against my salary while keeping the HISA funds available in my wife's name.
My questions are: Does this loan structure make sense, or is there a better way to structure it, without making it complex for a first time commercial purchase. I understand I won't have asset protection.
Has anyone financed a commercial property through ANZ Business Banking, and how was the experience? Would you recommend P&I for a first investment
Is there anything I'm overlooking from a lending or tax perspective?
I will be getting advice from my broker and accountant before proceeding, but I'm interested in hearing from others who have structured commercial property purchases in a similar way. Thanks in advance.

Redrawing those funds into a separate investment loan
You don't need to do that. Just pay the loan down to $100 left then redraw back into the offset and use the money to buy the warehouse its now an investment loan as far ATO is concerned and quite "clean".
The only issue I see potentially is that the home loan is probably in both your names? I'm not sure if what matters is the names on the loan or the names on the investment when it comes to allocating the interest.
Have you confirmed all likely costs for maintaining this investment (e.g. my friend had to install new AC at some point to the offices etc.)
[User #2272775775 postsjohnw2003Whirlpool Forums Addict] Improve writes...
looking at purchasing my first commercial warehouse as a long-term investment I would generally only recommend commercial property investment with a portfolio including a number of properties; not for only one property.
In difficult times, a commercial property can experience long vacant periods; this risk can be ameliorated with type and location diversification.
Historically, residential property has also gone through 10 year periods of stagnant of negative growth, & probably will again, although the occupancy isn’t so negatively impacted.
Has anyone financed a commercial property through ANZ Business Banking, and how was the experience? An associate, a long time ANZ customer recently applied for a low LVR loan with residential property as security; he wasted a huge amount of time to no avail & eventually gave up on ANZ.
I have been term in property building, development & investment.
Historically, Shares have been the far superior investment. Shares can fluctuate 25% in any one year, although there has never been a negative rolling 10 year period.

[User #78153599 postsxhd338Participant] this post was edited
You need to go see a specialized accountant or financial advisor on how to structure your new purchase, putting a commercial property into your personal name isn't something I would ever consider (I own multiple).
There's plenty of options available to help you minimize tax on this new investment, also you need to take into consideration any liabilities you have with the building, for instance if someone sues you for any reason (the owner of the building) then placing this asset in your personal name will effectively mean that all your personal assets (inc your PPOR) are now liable...
if you place it into your personal name and you're already a high income earner then effectively you could to be paying 45%+ on all income generated.
I don't know your circumstances/future plans as this hasn't been outlined in your original post, however I would speak to a financial advisor or specialized accountant about what structure would best suit your short or long term goals – some of them include:
Company
Trust
SMSF
They all have their advantages/disadvantages purely based on how your plan on what you wish to do with the income generated.
PS. You're probably buying at what I would call the worst time, the new CGT changes removed the opportunity for you to place the asset into a trust and gain access to a 50% discount after 12 months of ownership. I've never personally negatively geared a property, however this also adds to the fire for a lot of existing and new investors entering this space.
Growth rate of commercial/industrial buildings wont be the same, unless ofcourse this government gets the boot and the changes get reversed. It's simply not a viable investment in this day and age (this is my perspective of being in the market for over 15 years). You've got less hassle and you'll make more money by having your money sitting in a savings account.
4.65% is your annual return on that commercial property, that's NOT considering any repairs/maintanence and land tax, agent management fees, fire protection maintanence and body corporate fees (if applicable).
If your tenant is on a retail lease then you'll also cover land tax. You can earn 5%+ by having those funds in a savings account.... without any expenditure or liability.
The argument use-to be, "What about the capital gain". I personally believe that this is the end of commercial/industrial seeing a 5%-10% capital gain each year. I think you'll be lucky to see a 10% gain over the next 10 years. If you consider 10% of 650k which is 65k over 10 years then does it make it worth it? IMO – No it doesn't.
